Elicit
The practitioner first elicits or gathers information on what the client 
already knows about the nutrition or fitness topic. By finding out what the 
client already knows, you can learn about the client’s stage of change and 
identify any signs of hesitation toward behavior change.
Most important, when you do give information you can spend your 
time building on what your client already knows, instead of boring him 
with details he doesn’t need. In addition, the client may have misconcep-
tions about the topic. Eliciting his or her current understanding can clue 
you in to opportunities to later correct misunderstandings, if needed. (For 
more information on clarifying misinformation, see Chapter 12.)

Elicit
•• Ask the client what he already knows about the topic.
•• Ask the client what else he’d like to know about the topic.
•• Ask permission to provide information.
Provide
•• Share only relevant information.
•• Use the client’s experiences as a starting point and assess what is already known.
•• Keep it short and sweet.
•• Avoid using imperatives, such as “You should” or “All you need to do is. . . .”
Elicit
•• Check in with the client.
•• Invite the client to respond to the information provided by asking a question such as, 
“What are your thoughts on that?.”
